newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Social security a black hole in Argentine finances.
newsitem.headline: Social security a black hole in Argentine finances.

text.p: A financial crisis in Argentina's social security system that blighted state finances in 1996 will cause even more problems this year, analysts say.

"The social security deficit is getting bigger," Claudio Lozano, director of the Instituto de Estudios sobre Estado y Participacion, told Reuters. He added, "It is reasonable to expect that it will grow given that the causes of the imbalance are worsening."

Almost half of the 1996 fiscal deficit -- at $6 billion equivalent to around two percent of gross domestic product -- went to plugging financial holes in a state social security system with serious administrative problems and poor service.

Even though the system runs a permanent deficit, 75 percent of people on state pensions receive just about $300 a month, a fraction of the $1,000 a family needs to survive in Buenos Aires, according to consultants FIDE.

The social security system's administrative problems are not new, but the introduction in 1994 of a system of private pension funds diverted contributions from state coffers and has caused a chronic state of underfinancing. A cut in payroll tax made matters even worse.

"The cause of the fiscal deficit has a first name and a surname: the starting up of the private pension funds (AFJPs) and the reduction in payroll tax," Norberto Sosa, economist at the private Proeco consultancy, told Reuters.
The AFJPs now receive $3 billion a year which would otherwise have gone to the government. But the state still has to fork out pensions for people who have already retired.
When the AFJPs first started up, only 32.3 percent of workers opted out of the state system, but this proportion rose to almost 70 percent in 1996.

Contributions to the AFJPs totaled $179 million in June 1995, just slightly more than the $173 million received by the state. But by June 1996 the AFJPs received $220 million and the government only $126 million.

The social security system's financial deficit rose to 35 percent of its total budget in 1995, from 23 percent in 1993, according to Jorge Beinsten, a former director of planning at the Social Security Secretariat.

"The situation got worse as 1996 drew on," he said, explaining that the social security deficit reached $924 million, or 60 percent of its total budget by March. This was up from a deficit of 30 percent in March 1995.
But Lozano pointed out that the growing weight of the private pension system also perversely added to the state's means of financing.
"The private pension system knocks the social security system's finances out of balance, but then it finances the deficit by buying public bonds," he said.

At the same time as state pension contributions have fallen, a reduction in payroll tax in 1994 has also relieved state finances of $2.4 billion. Yet the government's hopes that lower payroll tax would boost employment have so far proved in vain.
Joblessness, now at 17.3 percent, also reduces the numbers of workers paying into the state social security system.

Another financial headache has come from the transferral of notoriously badly run provincial pensions to the federal government. Funding the provincial pensions should cost the government about $1 billion in 1997.
